2. The short fact leading to this revisional application is that the opposite party as petitioner filed the aforesaid miscellaneous case on 27.4.1994 and prayed for an injunction under section 41 (b) read with item 4 of the Second Schedule of the Arbitration Act, 1940 corresponding to section 12 (6) (g) of the English Arbitration Act, 1950 and prayer was made for an order of ad-interim injunction restraining the petitioner from giving effect to the notice of termination in question. 

 5. Mr. M Nurullah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, drawing our attention to the deed of agreement at the outset submitted that in the matter of arbitration both the parties agreed that the English Arbitration Act, 1950 shall be applicable and when Arbitration Agreement provides that the English law shall be applicable in the matter of Arbitration the injunction granted by the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka cannot be sustained. He submits that the petitioner Company is a British Company having its head office in London and the present opposite party is from Bangladesh and when the courts of both the countries have jurisdiction in the matter, by way of agreement the parties decided that in case of arbitration the English law shall apply. He submits that when consciously the parties agreed on a particular Arbitration law, only that law shall be applicable. He contends that in the agreement there is no total ouster of jurisdiction of either courts or the courts of this country and the stipulation in the agreement that English law of Arbitration will be applicable is not illegal and there is also no infringement of public policy in the matter. 

 7. Drawing our attention to certain Annexures Mr. Nurullah submits that the appointment of Mr. Justice Tofazzal Hossain Khan as Arbitrator is on the very face illegal and as his appointment cannot be construed as a valid and legal appointment the subsequent replacement by Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury is also illegal and that cannot be construed as a valid arbitration and, as such, there cannot be any injunction. Mr. Nurullah lastly submits that for getting an injunction under Arbitration Act, 1940 and Arbitration Act, 1950 a proceeding must be there in existence which is very much absent in the present case before us. 

 8. As against this Mr. Abdul Wadud Khondker, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, submits that when an Arbitration proceeding commences the court has the power to grant an injunction and arbitration commences from the date of issuance of notice. Here in this case a notice was issued appointing Mr. Justice Tofazzal Hossain Khan as the Arbitrator to which no objection was raised by the present petitioner and, as such, Mr. Khan entered reference, but subsequently he refused to complete the arbitration and in his place Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Choudhury was made an Arbitrator. So, when there is already an arbitration proceeding the learned Subordinate Judge acted within his jurisdiction in granting the injunction. He further submits that by agreement the court jurisdiction cannot be ousted. According to him, in the present case as the agreement was finally signed and executed at Dhaka and the business was transacted at Dhaka, payments were made here in Bangladesh, tickects are sold here in this country and the British Airways has a controlling office at Dhaka, the local court has jurisdiction in the matter. He submits that excepting the signing of the agreement by the British Airways in London nothing has been done at that place, everything was done in Bangladesh including the signing of agreement by the opposite party. He submits that under clause 14 of the Agreement in an indirect way the jurisdiction of the local courts have been ousted which is not supported by any law. According to Mr. Khondker, the consistent view of the higher courts of the subcontinent is that any such stipulation in the contract by' which the jurisdiction of a court is ousted shall be construed as void and the second part of Clause 14 of the present agreement suffers from that defect. According to Mr. Khondker, it is well settled that when an arbitration proceeding commences under the Arbitration Act, 1940 or even under the Arbitration Act, 1950 the court has the authority and jurisdiction to grant an injunction and here in the present case the learned Subordinate Judge rightly exercised that jurisdiction. 

 Heard the learned Counsel for the plaintiff petitioner. Perused the contents of the petition for injunction under section 41(b) read with Rule 4 of the Second Schedule of the Arbitration Act, 1940 corresponding to section 12(6) and Clause (g) of the Arbitration Act, 1950 (England) which have been supported by an affidavit, looked into the papers and documents filed vide firisti in support of the prayer embodied in the petition for injunction. Gone through the contents of the affidavit filed today Also have had a glimpse of the rulings and the relevant laws as referred to the court by the learned counsel during submission. The aforesaid injunction petition being found to have contained a prayer in it for restraining the opposite party defendant by an order of injunction from taking further step to give effect to the notice of termination till the arbitration is over, I am satisfied. Issue notice upon the opposite party defendant to show cause within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice as to why an order of temporary injunction in the manner sought for shall not be granted against him. In the meantime he is hereby restrained from giving effect to the notice of termination in question." 

 "Any difference or dispute concerning the scope, meaning, construction or effect of this Agreement, or any matter or thing contained herein or related hereto, shall be referred to Arbitration in accordance with, and subject to, the provisions of the Arbitration Act, 1950. The arbital award shall be final and conclusively binding upon the parties." 

 11. From this it appears that the English law of Arbitration was made applicable. Though it has not been specifically mentioned that English law of Arbitration shall apply but by the incorporation of the words "Arbitration Act, 1950", the English law of Arbitration was made applicable. 

 14. In the English Law of Arbitration (Arbitration Act of 1950) section 10 is the appropriate section. It provides that when an Arbitration Agreement provides that the reference shall be to a single Arbitrator, and all the parties do not, after differences have arisen, concur in the appointment of an arbitrator and if the appointment is not made within 7 clear days after the service of the notice, the High Court or a Judge thereof may, on application by the party who gave the notice appoint an arbitrator, umpire or third arbitrator who shall have the like powers to act in the reference and make an award as if he had been appointed by consent of all parties. 

 17. Admittedly, for an appointment of an arbitrator under Arbitration Act, 1940 a notice is required to be issued by one party to the other giving them 15 clear days' time from date of service to concur on the appointment. It appears from Annexure F filed by the opposite party that on 3.2.1994 they appointed Mr. Justice Tofazzal Hossain Khan, Senior Advocate of Bangladesh Supreme Court as an Arbitrator. In this Annexure F there is nothing asking" to concur the appointment of Mr. Justice Tofazzal Hossain Khan and it appears from Annexure H that in pursuance to this appointment Mr. TH Khan entered reference by notice dated 15.2.94. So, there is non-compliance of the provision on concurrence in the appointment of single arbitrator as requred under Arbitration Act, 1940. Admittedly, after the expiry of 15 clear days, the court was not moved for appointment of a single Arbitrator. It further appears from these that for appointment of single Arbitrator the provision of section 10 of the English Law of Arbitration, 1950 has also not been followed. 

 23. Mr. Abdul Wadud Khandker submits that when the opposite party issued a notice for appointment of an arbitrator or appointing an arbitrator the arbitration proceeding commences and in such a case the court has every jurisdiction to grant an injunction. We have gone through Halsbury's as well as Russell's commentaries. From these it appears that when one party give a notice on the other party requiring him or them to appoint an arbitrator the proceeding commenced. The use of the word "requiring" is significant here in the matter. The word "requiring or require" means to demand or to cancel. This indicates that these two commentaries have no manner of application in the case of single arbitrator. When in the agreement for arbitration there is mention of two or more arbitrators to be appointed by the respective parties and when one party gives notice appointing an arbitrator/arbitrators he may require the other party to appoint their arbitrator/arbitrators so that arbitration may proceed and that is meant only for saving limitation. So, these two commentaries cannot profitably be used in the present case before us as herein the present case the arbitration is to be conducted by a single arbitrator. It is true that a court may grant injunction when arbitration proceeding commenced but there must be a valid and legal commencement of arbitration. Where more than one arbitrator is required to be appointed, according to Russell and Halsbury the concurrence of the other party is not at all necessary. The law provides that if after the receipt of the notice within the stipulated time the other party does not appoint their arbitrator, the arbitrator so appointed will conclude the arbitration from which it appears that in those cases arbitration commences from the date of issuance of the notice. But in the case of single arbitrator concurrence of the other side is necessary both under the Arbitration Act, 1940 and English Law of Arbitration, 1950. In the present case in the aforesaid situation it cannot be found that arbitration proceeding has already commenced and the learned Subordinate Judge was right in passing the impugned order. In the case of a single arbitrator the arbitrator gets the authority to arbitrate on his formal appointment that is, either on the concurrence by the other side or on the appointment by the concerned court which is found to be very much lacking in the present case. 

 26. It appears from the agreement that both the parties agreed on the dispute. So, for appointment of an arbitrator the English Law and only the English Law shall be applicable which provides that either party may issue a notice on the other side asking them to concur on the appointment of arbitrator and if there is concurrence arbitration may proceed but if there is no concurrence the party who gave the notice may move the High Court or a Judge thereof, for such appointment. When the appointment of Mr. Justice Tofazzal Hossain Khan has not been made in pursuance to the provision of section 10 of the English Law of Arbitration it cannot be construed that he has been legally appointed or that he has legal authority to proceed, with the arbitration. The same is the case with Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury. If we consider Annexure L, the notice for concurrence, then also it would be found that it failed the test of section 10 of the English Law of Arbitration as this proposal was made on 26.4.94 and that before the expiry of 7 days the court was moved for injunction and we have already found that under section 41 of our Arbitration Act, 1940 injunction may be obtained when there is an Arbitration proceeding and we have already found that in such a case proceeding commences when the parties concurred or there was an appointment of an arbitrator through court. So, the appointment of Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury as an arbitrator suffers from inherent defect both under Arbitration Act, 1940 and the English Arbitration Act, 1950. 

 28. Further section 41(b) of the Arbitration Act empowers the court to grant injunction for the purpose of and in relation to arbitration proceedings. It has been held by the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Union of India vs. Raman Iron Foundry, reported in AIR 1974 (SC) 1265, that the court has power under section 41(b) of the Arbitration Act read with the Second Schedule to issue interim injunction but such interim injunction can only be for the purpose of and in relation to arbitration proceedings". The same is the view of this court expressed in the case of Sk. Deen Mohammad vs. Sk. Peer Mohammad, reported in 25 DLR 274, wherein a Division Bench of this court has held that the provision of section 41(b) of the Arbitration Act which entitled a party to an order of temporary or interim injunction under the provisions of law can also be granted injunction by the court when disputes are pending in an arbitration proceeding whether reference to such arbitration has been made without the intervention of the court, the rule of law must be the same for both. The Calcutta High Court in the case of Ranjit Chandra Mitter vs. Union of India reported in AIR 1963(Cal) 594, held that an interim relief under section 41 can only be asked for and granted by the court in some proceedings or in a pending suit and in the absence of such a proceeding an application under section 41 of the Arbitration Act is not maintainable. The consistent view of the higher courts of this subcontinent is that for getting an order of injunction under section 41(b) of the Arbitration Act of 1940 there must be a proceeding. But here in the present case before us we have already found that there is no proceeding in the eye of law for invoking the jurisdiction of the court under section 41 (b) of the Arbitration Act, 1940 or under any of the provisions of Arbitration Act, 1950. When there is no proceeding pending or no proceeding is there before the court the learned Subordinate Judge cannot grant an injunction invoking the jurisdiction under section 41(b) of the Arbitration Act and in that view of the matter we hold that the impugned order is bad in law and cannot be sustained.
